chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluwayh (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim quoted on the authority of al-Mukhtar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mukhtar al-Hamadani, on the authority of al-Fath ibn Yazid al-Gurgani, that he had heard Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) say:

Regarding God, the Exalted, the Glorious: He is the Subtle, the All-Aware, the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the One, the Only, the Self-Sufficient. He begets not, nor is He begotten, nor is there any equal to Him. He is the Originator of things, the Formator of bodies, the Depicter of images. If it were as they say, the Creator would not be distinguished from the created, nor the Maker from the made. There is a difference between Him and what He has formed, depicted, and originated, since nothing is similar to Him, and He is not similar to anything.

I said: Yes, may I be your ransom, but you said: The Only, the Self-Sufficient, and you said: He is not similar to anything. God is One, and man is also one. Is it not the case that their oneness is similar?

He said: O Fath, you are correct, may God make you firm. The similarity is in the meanings. As for the names, they are one and denote the named. This is because man, although called one, is informed to be a single body, not two. However, man himself is not one in essence, because his limbs are different and his colors are many and not one. He is composed of divided parts that are not equal; his blood is not his flesh, and his flesh is not his blood; his nerves are not his veins, his hair is not his skin, his blackness is not his whiteness. And so are all other creations. Therefore, man is one in name, but not one in meaning. God, the Exalted in Glory, is One, and there is no other one but Him. There is no difference in Him, no disparity, no addition, and no deficiency. As for man, the created, the manufactured, composed of different parts and various essences, although he is united as one thing.

I said: May I be your ransom, you have relieved me, may God relieve you. Your saying: The Subtle, the All-Aware, explain it to me as you explained the One, for I know that His subtleness is contrary to the subtleness of His creation in distinction, but I would like you to elaborate on that for me.

He said: O Fath, we only call Him Subtle because of His subtle creation and His knowledge of the subtle thing and the non-subtle thing. In the subtle creation among small animals are mosquitoes, gnats, and what is smaller than them, which the eyes hardly distinguish. Indeed, due to their smallness, the male is hardly distinguished from the female, and the newborn from the old. When we see their smallness in their subtleness, their guidance to mating, their escape from death, and their gathering of what suits them from the depths of the seas, the bark of trees, the deserts, and the wastelands, and their understanding of each other's speech, and what their children understand from them, and their carrying of nourishment to them, then the composition of their colors, red with yellow, and white with green, and what our eyes hardly distinguish with complete clarity, and our eyes do not see and our hands do not touch, we know that the Creator of this creation is Subtle. He was subtle in creating what we named without effort, tool, or instrument. And every maker of something creates from something, but God, the Creator, the Subtle, the Magnificent, created and made without being from something.
ai.seo_question: How does Imam al-Rida explain the meaning of 'Al-Latif' (The Subtle) in relation to God's creation and oneness?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) elucidates the divine attribute of *Al-Latif* by distinguishing between nominal oneness (*wahdaniyyah al-ism*) and essential oneness (*wahdaniyyah al-ma'*), arguing that while humans are composite and divisible, God is absolutely simple with no internal differentiation. He further explains that 'Subtle' denotes God's effortless creation of minute entities without material tools or instruments, contrasting His independent power with the derived, material-based craftsmanship of created beings. This discourse reinforces the Shia doctrine of *Tawhid al-Dhat* (Unity of Essence) against anthropomorphic views that attribute physical composition to the Divine.
